title: Character, feelings and weather
goal: Describe people and things, say how you feel, and talk about the weather, the number one conversation starter in Bandung.
bekal: Bandung weather and how to talk about it

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Rain on the porch
dialogs.intro: A rainy afternoon. Rani and Sari are stuck on the porch, and the talk drifts from the weather to the people around them.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Tuh, hujan deui. Unggal soré kieu, Téh.
lines.id: Look, it's raining again. Every afternoon it's like this.
lines.literal: there, rain again. every afternoon like-this, Téh.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Tiris pisan, euy. Di Jakarta mah tara sadingin ieu.
lines.id: It's so cold, wow. It's never this cold in Jakarta.
lines.literal: cold very, [euy]. in Jakarta [mah] never as-cold this.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Ieu mah kakara. Bulan Juli mah leuwih tiris deui.
lines.id: This is just the start. July is even colder.
lines.literal: this [mah] just. month July [mah] more cold again.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Aduh. Kuring kudu meuli jakét nu kandel.
lines.id: Oh no. I need to buy a thick jacket.
lines.literal: oh-no. I must buy jacket that thick.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Ka Bu Éha waé nanya, manéhna mah nyaho toko nu murah.
lines.id: Just ask Bu Éha, she knows a cheap shop.
lines.literal: to Bu Éha just ask, she [mah] know shop that cheap.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Bu Éha téh bageur pisan nya. Kamari mah dibéré kuéh.
lines.id: Bu Éha is so kind, isn't she? Yesterday she gave me cake.
lines.literal: Bu Éha [téh] kind very [nya]. yesterday [mah] given cake.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Heueuh, daréhdéh ka saha waé. Béda jeung tatangga nu ditu.
lines.id: Yes, she's friendly to everyone. Not like the neighbor over there.
lines.literal: yes, friendly to who just. different with neighbor that at there.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Nu mana? Nu imahna gedé téa?
lines.id: Which one? The one with the big house?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Heueuh. Rada sombong. Disapa gé sok teu ngawaler.
lines.id: Yes. A bit stuck-up. Even when you greet him, he often doesn't answer.
lines.literal: yes. somewhat arrogant. greeted also like not answer.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Ah, sugan waé keur seueur pikiran.
lines.id: Oh, maybe he just has a lot on his mind.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Tuh, Téh Rani mah hadé haté. Kuring mah geus pundung ti baheula.
lines.id: See, you're so good-hearted, Rani. I'd have been sulking ages ago.
lines.literal: there, Téh Rani [mah] good heart. I [mah] already sulk from before.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hahaha. Hayu ah, urang nyieun bandrék. Tiris teuing ieu mah.
lines.id: Hahaha. Come on, let's make some bandrek. It's freezing.
lines.literal: hahaha. come-on ah, we make bandrek. cold too-much this [mah].

notes: **Bageur** = kind, good-natured. ⚠️ It describes **character**, not looks. For things that are good, use *alus*/*saé*. Together with *cageur, bener, pinter, singer*, it's one of the five ideal Sundanese qualities.
**Daréhdéh** = friendly, quick to smile, easy to talk to. There's no single English word for it, and it's a very common compliment.

**Pundung** = to sulk because you're offended, usually in silence rather than open anger. It's the most typically Sundanese feeling word, and people often use it half-jokingly about themselves, as Sari does here.
**Hadé haté** literally "good heart," used for someone who doesn't think badly of others. Slightly different from *bageur*, which is more about deeds.
**Sugan** = maybe, perhaps, who knows. It carries a note of hope: *sugan waé* = let's hope so. Other words for possibility: *meureun* (probably), *sigana* (it seems).
**Kandel** = thick; its opposite is **ipis** (thin). Both are worth learning as a pair.

grammars.title: Comparing: leuwih, pang-…-na, sa-…-na
body: Sundanese comparisons use three patterns. None of them change the adjective itself; you just add small words or affixes around it.
after: **Ti batan** = than (loma); the lemes is also **ti batan**, or **tibatan**. In conversation you'll often hear it without *batan* at all: *manéhna leuwih jangkung ti kuring* = he's taller than me.

⚠️ Watch the **sa-…-na** pattern, because it looks like the possessive ending *-na*. *Sadinginna* doesn't mean "its coldness" but "as cold as that." Context always makes it clear, but don't be surprised when you see it.

For "more and more," Sundanese uses **beuki**: *beuki tiris* (colder and colder), *beuki lila beuki alus* (the longer, the better). In other uses the same word means "to like, be fond of"; context tells them apart.

blocks.text: **Someah hade ka semah** (warm and kind to guests) is one of the sayings Sundanese people quote most often to describe themselves. If you want to pay a host a compliment that really lands, this is the one.

To say how you feel, the order is the same as in English: pronoun + feeling, with no "am": *Abdi bungah pisan* (I'm very happy). To ask: **Kumaha raosna?** (how does it feel) or, more casually, **Kumaha, betah?** (so, feeling at home?)

⚠️ In Sundanese, **gelap** means **thunder and lightning**, not "dark" as in Indonesian. The word for dark is **poék**. It's one of the easiest trap words to trip over: *ulah kaluar, aya gelap* = "don't go out, there's lightning."

blocks.title: Talking about the weather
items: **Tiis pisan poé ieu nya.** — It's really cold today, isn't it?
**Hujan ti tadi teu eureun-eureun.** — It hasn't stopped raining all day.
**Halodo pisan minggu ieu.** — It's been scorching this week.
**Kade kahujanan.** — Mind you don't get caught in the rain.
**Bawa payung, sugan waé hujan.** — Take an umbrella, in case it rains.

items: How you feel meeting an old friend: ____
